label: Tectonic Origin and Geomorphological Classification
info: The Himalayas are Tertiary-era young fold mountains formed by the ongoing continental collision of the Indian Plate with the Eurasian Plate that commenced ~50–60 million years ago. India's relief encompasses three mountain generations: Archaean relict residual mountains (Aravallis), fault-block horsts and escarpments (Satpuras and Western Ghats), and Alpine-Himalayan compressional fold systems.

label: Nodal Ministries and Central Departments
info: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC); Ministry of Earth Sciences (MoES); Ministry of Mines; and Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region (MDoNER). Specialized research and glaciological monitoring are steered by the Wadia Institute of Himalayan Geology (WIHG, Dehradun), Geological Survey of India (GSI, Kolkata), National Centre for Polar and Ocean Research (NCPOR, Goa), and G.B. Pant National Institute of Himalayan Environment (NIHE, Almora).

label: Key Flagship Reports and Atlases
info: Glacial Lake Atlas of Indian Himalayan River Basins (Central Water Commission - CWC); Landslide Atlas of India (National Remote Sensing Centre - NRSC, ISRO); Disaster Management Plan for Indian Himalayan Region (National Disaster Management Authority - NDMA); and the Biennial India State of Forest Report (ISFR by Forest Survey of India - FSI).

label: Major Structural Tectonic Sutures and Faults
info: The Himalayan orogenic belt is bounded and stratified from north to south by major tectonic boundaries: Indus-Tsangpo Suture Zone (ITSZ), Main Central Thrust (MCT, separating Greater from Lesser Himalayas), Main Boundary Thrust (MBT, separating Lesser Himalayas from Shiwaliks), and the Himalayan Frontal Thrust (HFT, separating Shiwaliks from the Indo-Gangetic Alluvium).

label: Trans-Himalayan Mountain System
info: Situated immediately north of the Great Himalayan Range; predominantly composed of marine fossiliferous Tethyan sedimentary strata underlain by Tertiary granites. Encompasses the Karakoram Range, Ladakh Range, and Zaskar Range. Houses the world's second-highest peak, K2/Godwin-Austen (8,611 m), along with giant non-polar glaciers including Siachen (76 km), Baltoro, Biafo, and Hispar.

label: Greater Himalayas (Himadri) - Structural Anatomy
info: The most continuous, lofty, and ancient crystalline ridge; average elevation ~6,000 m. Formed of Archaean granites, gneisses, and high-grade metamorphics. Houses the highest Indian-administered summit, Mount Kanchenjunga (8,586 m, Sikkim), as well as prominent summits like Nanda Devi (7,816 m, Uttarakhand), Kamet, Makalu, and Dhaulagiri.

label: Syntaxial Bends of the Himalayas
info: The east-west trending Himalayan arc terminates abruptly at two sharp knee-bend tectonic flexures known as syntaxial bends: the Western Syntaxis anchored around Nanga Parbat (where the Indus River cuts an 8,000-ft deep canyon) and the Eastern Syntaxis anchored around Namcha Barwa (where the Tsangpo-Brahmaputra turns south into India through the Dihang gorge).

label: Lesser Himalayas (Himachal) and Crystalline Nappes
info: Runs parallel to the Himadri with average elevations between 3,700 m and 4,500 m and widths of 60–80 km. Composed of altered sedimentary and metamorphic rocks forming complex allochthonous nappes. Principal ranges include the Pir Panjal Range (longest, breached by the Jhelum and Chenab rivers), Dhauladhar Range, Nag Tibba, and the Mahabharat Lekh.

label: Longitudinal Tectonic Valleys: Duns and Chos
info: Located between the Lesser Himalayas and the Shiwalik Range; flat-bottomed structural depressions filled with coarse consolidated Pleistocene gravels and alluvium, known as 'Duns' in the west (e.g., Dehradun, Kotli Dun, Patli Dun) and 'Duars' in the east. Seasonal torrential rain-fed braided streams that dissect and erode Shiwalik slopes are locally designated as 'Chos' in Punjab and Haryana.

label: Shiwalik Range (Outer Himalayas)
info: The outermost, youngest Himalayan foothills, with elevations of 900–1,100 m. Composed of unconsolidated Tertiary sandstones, conglomerates, and lacustrine gravels brought down by Himalayan rivers. Extremely fragile, seismically vulnerable, and prone to severe gully erosion and shallow landslides.

label: Karewa Formations of the Kashmir Himalayas
info: Lacustrine, fluvio-glacial, and aeolian silt-clay deposits lining the intermontane Jhelum basin between the Pir Panjal and Zaskar ranges. Dating to the Plio-Pleistocene era, these elevated flat terraces provide the unique micro-pedo-climatic habitat essential for the GI-tagged cultivation of Kashmiri saffron (Zafran), walnuts, and almonds.

label: Purvanchal (Eastern Hills)
info: The southward continuation of the Himalayan orogeny past the Dihang gorge along the Myanmar border; composed mostly of Tertiary sandstones. Encompasses the Patkai Bum (Arunachal Pradesh), Naga Hills (housing Saramati Peak, 3,826 m), Barail Range, Manipur Hills, and the Mizo/Lushai Hills (housing Phawngpui/Blue Mountain, 2,157 m). Characterized by parallel ridge-and-valley topography and synclinal anticlinal folds.

label: Geomorphological Status of the Meghalaya Plateau
info: Topographically elevated (~600–1,800 m) but geologically NOT part of the Himalayan fold system. It is a detached, uplifted horst block of the Archaean Peninsular Gneissic Complex, separated from the Rajmahal Hills and Chota Nagpur Plateau by the Garo-Rajmahal Gap (Malda Fault / Malda Trough). Encompasses the Garo, Khasi (Shillong Peak, 1,961 m), and Jaintia hills.

label: Strategic Passes (La) Across the Himalayas
info: Karakoram Pass (Ladakh to Tarim Basin); Zoji La (Kashmir Valley to Ladakh); Banihal Pass/Jawaharlal Tunnel (Jammu to Srinagar across Pir Panjal); Shipki La (Himachal to Tibet, through which the Sutlej enters); Lipulekh (Uttarakhand-Tibet tri-junction, Mansarovar route); Nathu La and Jelep La (Sikkim to Chumbi Valley); and Bomdi La (Arunachal Pradesh to Lhasa).

label: Aravalli Range - Oldest Relict Orogeny
info: Dating to the Proterozoic/Precambrian era (~1.5–2 billion years ago), the Aravallis represent one of the world's oldest relict fold mountain systems, deeply eroded down to residual monadnocks. Extends ~800 km from Palanpur in Gujarat through Rajasthan to Delhi Ridge. Guru Shikhar (1,722 m) on the Mount Abu granitic pluton is its highest elevation; acts as a regional drainage divide between the Indus and Ganga basins.

label: Vindhyan Mountain Range
info: A non-folded relict sandstone-shale escarpment running parallel to the north of the Narmada River for ~1,200 km (from Jobat in Gujarat to Sasaram in Bihar). Forms the primary physical and cultural watershed between Indo-Gangetic North India and Peninsular South India. Average elevation is 300–650 m; famous for historic building materials and the diamondiferous Panna conglomerate belt.

label: Satpura Range - True Tectonic Horst
info: A tectonic horst mountain block bounded by two major rift-valley grabens: the Narmada Rift to the north and the Tapi Rift to the south. Comprises a sequence of ranges from west to east: the Rajpipla Hills, Gawilgarh Hills, Mahadeo Hills (housing the Pachmarhi biosphere and the highest peak Dhupgarh, 1,350 m), and the Maikal Range.

label: Amarkantak Plateau - Radial Drainage Center
info: The eastern node of the Maikal Range where the Vindhyan and Satpura systems converge. Functions as a significant radial drainage hub in Peninsular India: the Narmada flows west into the Arabian Sea, the Son flows northeast to join the Ganga, and the Hasdeo/Mahanadi system drains southeast toward the Bay of Bengal.

label: Western Ghats (Sahyadris) - Continental Escarpment
info: Stretches ~1,600 km continuously from the south of Tapi River down to Kanyakumari. It is not a true fold mountain, but the elevated, faulted, and heavily eroded western rift-shoulder of the Peninsular Deccan Plateau, created during the breakup of Gondwanaland. Recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the world's eight 'Hottest Hotspots' of biological diversity.

label: Orography and Peak Altitudes of the Western Ghats
info: Divided into Northern Sahyadris (basaltic/Deccan trap composition; highest peak Kalsubai at 1,646 m), Central Sahyadris (granitic-gneissic; housing Kudremukh, 1,892 m), and Southern Sahyadris. The highest peak in Peninsular India is Anamudi (2,695 m) in the Anaimalai Hills of Kerala, followed by Meesapulimala (2,640 m).

label: Orogenic Mountain Gaps in the Western Ghats
info: Major natural structural breaches across the continuous Sahyadrian ridge: Thal Ghat / Kasara Ghat (links Mumbai to Nashik/Kolkata); Bhor Ghat (links Mumbai to Pune/Chennai); and the Palghat Gap / Palakkad Gap (a 30-km wide tectonic shear fracture separating the Nilgiris from the Anaimalai Hills, linking Kerala to Coimbatore and Tamil Nadu).

label: Nilgiri Hills - Mountain Knot of the Peninsula
info: The orographic knot where the Western Ghats converge with the Eastern Ghats. Composed of high-grade charnockite massifs. The highest peak is Doddabetta (2,637 m). Houses India's first designated Biosphere Reserve (Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve, established 1986 under UNESCO MAB).

label: Eastern Ghats - Dissected Relict Morphology
info: A discontinuous, heavily denuded, and faulted ancient Precambrian mobile belt running along the Bay of Bengal coast from Odisha to Tamil Nadu. Dissected into isolated massifs by major east-flowing rivers (Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Cauvery). Highest recorded elevations are Jindhagada Peak (1,690 m) in the Araku Valley (Andhra Pradesh) and Arma Konda (1,680 m).

label: Southern Relict Hills of Tamil Nadu
info: Fragmented southern remnants of the Eastern Ghats complex: Shevaroy Hills (Yercaud plateau), Javadi Hills, Pachaimalai, and Kolli Hills. Dominated by Archaean charnockites and bauxite caps, these dry deciduous and scrub-covered uplands form prominent rain-shadow plateaus.

label: Cryospheric Glacial Dynamics and GLOF Risks
info: The Himalayas constitute the 'Third Pole', supporting >33,000 sq km of glacier cover. Warming at rates above the global average has caused sustained negative glacier mass balances, leading to the rapid expansion of moraine-dammed proglacial lakes. As highlighted in the CWC Glacial Lake Atlas and NDMA protocols, this dramatically escalates the hazard of Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs), as witnessed at South Lhonak Lake (Sikkim, 2023) and Kedarnath/Chorabari (2013).

label: Seismic Zonation and Landslide Susceptibility
info: Due to ongoing northward plate convergence (~4–5 cm/year), the entire Himalayan arc falls into the highest seismic risk zones (Seismic Zone V and Zone IV of BIS 1893). As documented in the ISRO Landslide Atlas of India, Himalayan districts (e.g., Rudraprayag, Tehri Garhwal) and Western Ghats escarpments (e.g., Wayanad) experience the highest national landslide density, aggravated by tectonic shear, slope overloading, and extreme rainfall events.
